items.label: section_header
items.text: HINT

items.label: text
items.text: You now have two definitions of oxidation (and its reverse, reduction). Which one should you use? Use whichever is simpler in the case you are asked about! Both definitions are true. Don't worry too much about this at the moment. With a little experience, you will find it is obvious which one you need to use in various cases.

items.label: text
items.text: The Zn atoms are oxidised to Zn²+ ions because they lose electrons. The Cu²+ ions gain electrons and are reduced to Cu atoms. We can split up the ionic equation to show the individual oxidation and reduction processes:

items.label: formula
items.text: Z n ( s ) & \to Z n ^ { 2 + ( a q ) } + 2 e ^ { - \text {expiration} } \\ C u ^ { 2 + ( a q ) } + 2 e ^ { - } & \to C u ( s ) \text { reduction}

items.label: text
items.text: Thet     e  se sa e  e tihe processes (either oxidation or reduction) occurring in the reaction. In reality, these processes cannot occur one without the other: if something gains electrons, it has to get them from somewhere, so something else must lose electrons.

items.label: text
items.text: A couple more definitions (this time in terms of electrons):

items.label: list_item
items.text: An oxidising agent is something that oxidises something else by taking electrons away from it. Oxidising agents accept electrons and therefore are reduced in a reaction.

items.label: list_item
items.text: A reducing agent is something that reduces something else by giving electrons to it. Reducing agents give away electrons and therefore are oxidised in a reaction.

items.label: text
items.text: Let us look again at the overall ionic equation for the displacement reaction between zinc and copper ions:

items.label: formula
items.text: Z n ( s ) + C u ^ { 2 + } ( a q ) \rightarrow Z n ^ { 2 + } ( a q ) + C u ( s )

items.label: text
items.text: The Zn reduces the Cu²+ by giving electrons to it and therefore the Zn is the reducing agent. In the process of the reaction the Zn is oxidised because it has given electrons away (lost them).

items.label: text
items.text: The Cu²+ oxidises the Zn by taking electrons away from it, therefore the Cu²+ is the oxidising agent. In the process the Cu²+ is reduced because it has taken electrons (gained them).

items.label: section_header
items.text: THE REACTION BETWEEN COPPER AND SILVER NITRATE SOLUTION

items.label: text
items.text: Silver is below copper in the reactivity series, so a coil of copper wire in silver nitrate solution will produce metallic silver. Figure 14.7 shows the silver being produced as a mixture of grey 'fur' and delicate crystals. Notice the solution becoming blue, as copper(Ill) nitrate is produced:

items.label: formula

items.label: text
items.text: This time the nitrate ions are spectator ions, and the final version of the ionic equation looks like this:

items.label: formula
items.text: C u ( s ) + 2 A g ^ { + } ( a q ) \rightarrow C u ^ { 2 + } ( a q ) + 2 A g ( s )

items.label: text
items.text: This is another redox reaction.

items.label: text
items.text: The Cu is the reducing agent (it is oxidised) because it gives electrons to the Ag⁺ ions to reduce them to Ag. The Ag+ ion is the oxidising agent (it is reduced) because it takes electrons away from the Cu atoms.
